extracted.intended_audience: activity comptrollers, contracting officers, and government procurement managers implementing OMB Circular A-76 commercial activity studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and decision criteria for evaluating whether government activities should be contracted out under OMB Circular A-76, including processes for inventory, management review, cost comparison, contract award, and contract administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation method characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiation is used whenever sealed bid criteria cannot be met; characterized by bargaining and revision of offers; negotiation is between the Government and the contractor; multiple contractors do not usually negotiate simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bargaining usually applies to price, schedule, type of contract or proposed terms. Contractors are required to submit cost and pricing data used by Contracting Officers in negotiating prices and other terms when the cost of the contract exceeds $500,000.00.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exceptions allowing sole-source contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Competition in Contracting Act there are seven statutory exceptions which allow for sole source contracting; these contracts must be formally justified and receive an appropriate level of approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seven statutory exceptions include: (1) Only one responsible source; (2) Unusual or compelling urgency; (3) Industrial mobilization purposes; (4) Based on an international agreement or Foreign Military Sales requirement; (5) To meet a statutory requirement; (6) In the interest of national security; (7) In the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special contracting methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Special methods (multi-year contracting, options, leader company contracting) are available to increase economic efficiency through special contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method has specific limitations, objectives and requirements; selection of contracting method is only one part of acquisition — choosing the appropriate type of contract and applying its requirements is also essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key factors for selecting the type of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Several key factors should be taken into account when negotiating the type of contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most important factors include: (1) Price competition; (2) Cost analysis; (3) Price analysis; (4) Urgency of requirement; (5) Type and complexity of the requirement; (6) Adequacy of contractor's accounting system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm Fixed-Price Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm Fixed Price Contract — Government and contractor agree to a fixed price for goods or services not subject to adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places maximum risk on the contractor, who assumes full responsibility for cost control and any loss or profit; provides maximum incentive for the contractor to control costs. [Ref. 3:p. 16-2]

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Redeterminable Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-Price Redeterminable Contract — used when uncertainties preclude a firm fixed-price contract; provides a firm fixed price for an initial period and redetermination for subsequent periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key requirement is that the contractor must have an acceptable cost accounting system capable of accurately capturing and reporting costs to be used in subsequent redeterminations of price. [Ref. 3:p. 16-4]

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Incentive Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-Price Incentive Contract — contractor and Government agree on target costs and establish a pricing agreement that incentivizes cost reduction through a predetermined share formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contractor delivers under target cost, they share savings via additional profit; cost overrun reduces profit. There is a negotiated price ceiling. Can be divided into firm target or successive targets depending on cost/profit targets. [Ref. 3:p. 16-4]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Incentive-Fee Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost-Plus-Incentive-Fee — specifies a target cost, target profit, minimum and maximum fees and a fee adjustment formula; used for high risk efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows an initial negotiated fee later adjusted by a formula based on allowable vs. target costs; similar to fixed-price incentive but with no price ceiling; normally used for test and development contracts and encourages cost control during high-risk projects. [Ref. 3:p. 16-10]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Fee-Award Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost-Plus-Fee-Award — cost-reimbursement contract providing a base fixed fee plus an award amount based on excellence (quality, timeliness, technical ingenuity, cost-effective management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows Government flexibility to realign weights assigned to the award-fee formula at the beginning of each award period to alter emphasis on performance. [Ref. 3:p. 16-10]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee Contract characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee — provides the contractor a fixed fee in addition to reimbursement for allowable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually utilized where there are great risks and uncertainties, such as research and development work. [Ref. 3:p. 16]

rubrics_metrics.name: Other contract types and typical uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Other contracts/agreements include indefinite quantity contracts, definite quantity contracts, requirements contracts, time and materials contracts, labor hour contracts, letter contracts, basic ordering agreements, and blanket purchase agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each has particular uses — e.g., when exact quantity or time of delivery is unknown, small purchases, repetitive procurement of selected services or goods, or other peculiarities. Evaluate government needs and contractor abilities prior to selecting type. [Ref. 3:p. 16-2]

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-component contracting process
rubrics_metrics.description: The contracting process consists of six basic components: planning; source solicitation; source evaluation and selection; negotiation; award; contract administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning includes procurement method, acquisition strategy, contract type, solicitation development, evaluation of specs, circulation of draft RFPs, and determination of data needed for negotiation. Source solicitation covers release and modifications of solicitation and bidder's conferences. Source evaluation/selection involves evaluating bids/offers, determining lowest responsive and responsible bidder/offeror, establishing competitive range, applying source selection criteria, and preparing for negotiations using cost/price analysis and contractor data. Negotiation addresses delivery schedule, costs, pricing structure, profit/fee, and technical aspects. Award includes final agreement, contract preparation, legal review, signatures, and publicizing the award. Contract administration includes monitoring contractor performance, production surveillance, quality assurance, cost auditing, termination settlements, property management, and payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity comptroller role and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity comptroller must be aware of the contracting process, methods, types of contracts, and applicable laws and regulations; primary mission is efficient and economical use of government funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comptroller must monitor requisitioning, acquisition, and contracting processes, actively seek ways to decrease costs, provide technical guidance for financial matters, budget formulation, program review and promote economy and efficiency; may administer A-76 program or support Management Engineering analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 policy is based on three principles: (1) Achieve economy and enhance productivity; (2) Retain governmental functions in-house; (3) Rely on the commercial sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever an in-house function can be performed by commercial sector, compare contracting vs. in-house cost. Certain functions are inherently governmental and must be retained in-house. Government will not start commercial activities if commercial sources can provide more economically. [Ref. 6:p. 2]

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of the A-76 implementation process
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 process for conversion consists of four phases: inventory, management review, cost comparison, and implementation of cost comparison results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phases vary slightly between existing activities and new requirements; follow the prescribed steps and milestones; agencies typically designate a department to coordinate and monitor commercial activity milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) / Statement of Work (SOW) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The task analysis identifies function and tasks; from this a Statement of Work (SOW) is created which becomes the Performance Work Statement (PWS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS is the basis of both Government and commercial cost estimates and solicitation documents; its accuracy and scope must be flawless to obtain true estimates of cost for performance of equal work. Concurrently develop a Quality Assurance plan to ensure proper performance by commercial source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) development and use
rubrics_metrics.description: An indepth analysis of the organization and staffing leads to establishment of a Most Efficient Organization (MEO) — a streamlined organization to perform the mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO results are used to determine government in-house costs and become the baseline for comparisons; MEO may lead to cost decreases or personnel reductions; once completed, MEO is turned over to contracting activity in form of a sealed bid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation disclosure and displaced employee requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When contracting out, solicitation must notify contractors that award is based solely on a cost comparison between commercial bidders and government's MEO estimate and may be canceled if government's cost is lower; contractor must offer employment to any qualified government employee displaced by the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stipulation makes contractors aware of cancellation risk and protects displaced government employees by requiring offer of employment to qualified individuals. [Ref. 7:p. 41]

rubrics_metrics.name: Award thresholds and bid evaluation margins
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of commercial bids, bids are compared to MEO costs; contractor proposals must be at least ten percent less than the MEO to be judged a winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-year funding, bids will be for a minimum of three years. For single year funding, bids will cover two fiscal years after the initial year. Activities remaining in-house must be re-reviewed five years after the original study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for returning a commercial activity to in-house performance
rubrics_metrics.description: To reclaim a contracted activity, a new MEO must demonstrate that performing the activity in-house would be ten percent cheaper than the cost charged by the commercial source plus 25% of the commercial source's capital assets cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally contractor had to bid ten percent below government cost to win. To take contract back, government must be ten percent below the figure used to justify transfer — effectively requiring at least ~20% improvement versus original MEO. Approval authority for returning an activity rests with the Secretary or Director of the department or agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision criteria for existing services (A-76 Table I)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 13-step decision sequence for existing services determines eligibility for conversion and whether to conduct cost comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key decision questions include: Is activity a governmental function? Is it scheduled for inventory? Is it scheduled for review? Is in-house performance required for national defense? Is in-house performance at a government hospital required by agency medical director? Are satisfactory commercial sources available? Would unacceptable delay occur? Will contract be awarded under a Preferential Procurement Program (PPP)? Are less than ten FTEs present? Does Assistant Secretary waive cost comparison? Will contract cost be unreasonable? Conduct the cost comparison. Is the contract cost less than in-house cost by the specified margin? Activities deemed governmental are retained in-house and review stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision criteria for new services (A-76 Table II)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-step sequence for new requirements to determine whether to award a contract or conduct cost comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps include: Is activity a governmental function? Is in-house performance required for national defense? Is in-house performance at a government hospital required by agency medical director? Is a satisfactory commercial source available? Will contract be awarded under PPP? Will contract costs be unreasonable? Conduct cost comparison? Is contract cost less than in-house cost by the specified margin? For new services, award if total contract costs are less than in-house estimates by ten percent of personnel costs and less than twenty-five percent of acquisition costs of equipment and plant necessary to perform the service. [Ref. 5:p. A-1]

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory categorization by FTE for review prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventory of commercial activities separates functions into groups with 10 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) work years and those with more than 10 FTEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One FTE equals roughly one employee. Activities with less than 10 FTEs should be considered for conversion to commercial sources if costs are reasonable. Management reviews and scheduling depend on this categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management review purpose and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Management review phase examines whether reasons exist to preclude commercial performance and leads to establishment of an MEO and in-house cost estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews identify potential unacceptable delays, PPP applicability, necessity of in-house performance for defense or medical requirements, and produce the MEO which is then used as baseline for cost comparison. Proper planning and preparation is required to ensure review quality and accuracy of cost data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for quality assurance plan
rubrics_metrics.description: A Quality Assurance plan for a possible commercial service contract must be designed concurrently with the SOW/PWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to provide a course of action for the Government to ensure the activity is performed properly by the commercial source; QA plan is integral to accurate solicitation and performance monitoring.
